content: Heart sounds are the auditory phenomena produced by the beating heart and the flow of blood through its chambers and valves. These sounds, commonly referred to as the heartbeat, are assessed during cardiac auscultation using a stethoscope. This examination provides critical insights into the functional state of the heart. In healthy adults, two primary heart sounds are typically heard: the first heart sound (S1), often described as lub, and the second heart sound (S2), described as dub. These sounds occur sequentially with each heartbeat. In addition to these normal sounds, other auditory phenomena, such as heart murmurs and adventitious sounds, may be present. Heart murmurs result from turbulent blood flow, which can occur either within the heart or in its surrounding structures. Murmurs may be classified as physiological (benign) or pathological (abnormal). Pathological murmurs can arise from conditions such as valve stenosis, which restricts the opening of a valve and creates turbulence, or valve insufficiency (regurgitation), which allows blood to flow backward when the valve fails to close properly. The timing and location of murmurs within the cardiac cycle depend on their underlying cause. This sudden cessation of flow generates vibrations within the blood and surrounding structures, producing the S1 sound. Second Heart Sound (S2) Dub The second heart sound, S2, occurs at the end of ventricular systole, marking the beginning of diastole. The S2 sound results from the vibrations caused by the abrupt cessation of blood flow. Splitting of the Second Heart Sound Physiologic Splitting: This results in a physiologic splitting of S2, which is most pronounced during inspiration and best heard at the left second intercostal space. During expiration, the interval between A2 and P2 shortens, and the sounds may merge. Persistent Splitting: Persistent splitting of S2 occurs in conditions such as right bundle branch block (RBBB) and pulmonary hypertension. Paradoxical Splitting: This paradoxical splitting is more evident during expiration. Fixed Splitting: Fixed splitting of S2, which does not vary with respiration, is typically associated with atrial septal defects (ASD) or ventricular septal defects (VSD). Loud P2 A loud pulmonary component of S2 (P2) is most commonly associated with pulmonary hypertension. Extra Heart Sounds Occasionally, additional heart sounds may be heard, either in normal or pathological conditions. These include the third heart sound (S3) and the fourth heart sound (S4), which may indicate specific cardiac abnormalities. Third Heart Sound (S3) The third heart sound, S3, occurs during early diastole, shortly after S2. It is caused by the rapid deceleration of blood flow into a noncompliant left ventricle. S3 is often described as a ventricular gallop and produces a rhythm resembling the word Kentucky. While S3 may be normal in individuals under 40 years of age, its presence in older adults is typically pathological, often indicating left ventricular dysfunction or heart failure. Conditions associated with S3 include:g., post-myocardial infarction, dilated cardiomyopathy) Fourth Heart Sound (S4) The fourth heart sound, S4, occurs just before S1, during late diastole. It is caused by atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff or hypertrophic left ventricle. S4 is described as an atrial gallop and produces a rhythm resembling the word Tennessee. S4 is always pathological in adults and is associated with conditions such as: Long-standing hypertension Aortic stenosis Left ventricular hypertrophy Coronary artery disease Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Pulmonary hypertension Summation Gallop At rapid heart rates, S3 and S4 may merge into a single sound, known as a summation gallop. Abnormal Heart Sounds Heart murmurs are abnormal sounds caused by turbulent blood flow. They are often described as whooshing noises and may result from valve abnormalities or structural defects. Common murmurs include: Mitral Regurgitation: A systolic murmur caused by backward flow through the mitral valve. Aortic Stenosis: A systolic ejection murmur due to restricted aortic valve opening. Aortic Regurgitation: A diastolic murmur caused by backward flow through the aortic valve. Mitral Stenosis: A low-pitched diastolic murmur caused by restricted mitral valve opening. Adventitious Sounds Clicks: High-pitched sounds caused by conditions such as mitral valve prolapse or bicuspid aortic valve. Rubs: Pericardial friction rubs, associated with pericarditis, produce a scratching or creaking sound due to inflamed pericardial layers rubbing against each other. Surface Anatomy and Auscultation Heart sounds are best heard at specific anatomical locations downstream from the valves: Aortic Valve: Right second intercostal space Pulmonic Valve: Left second intercostal space Tricuspid Valve: Left fourth intercostal space Mitral Valve: Left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line Recording Heart Sounds Modern electronic stethoscopes allow for the recording and playback of heart sounds, enabling detailed analysis of low-frequency murmurs and other abnormalities. Treatment Abnormal heart sounds themselves do not require treatment. Instead, the underlying cardiac condition must be addressed to resolve the abnormality.
